title: AgentSelect: Benchmark for Narrative Query-to-Agent Recommendation
one_liner: Turn agent selection into a recommendation problem where a user's narrative request must be matched to an agent's capability profile, not just to a popular identifier.
lead: As more deployable agents appear, choosing the right one becomes a problem of recommendation. A user writes a narrative request such as 'summarize legal emails and draft a reply with citations,' and the system must recommend a full agent configuration that can actually do that job. Existing benchmarks do not test this well because they score isolated components and rarely provide query-conditioned supervision for end-to-end agent choice. AgentSelect builds that missing benchmark.

problem.h2: Picking a deployable agent is different from ranking a single model
paras: A deployable agent is more than one model. It can include prompts, tools, routing rules, and other configuration choices that determine what tasks it can do in practice. Existing leaderboards usually score one part at a time, such as language quality or one tool benchmark, so they do not directly teach how to choose a full agent for a user's request.

The supervision is also sparse in a difficult way. Many recommendation systems work well when the same popular items are chosen again and again. In agent recommendation, a long narrative request may point to a rarely chosen agent with a very specific capability mix. That makes simple identifier-based methods fragile, because the system must understand the request content and the agent profile instead of relying on repeated popularity.

callout.html: Treat the task as query-to-agent recommendation, because the recommender must map user intent to agent capabilities under long-tail supervision.

steps.text: Gather benchmark results and marketplace-style descriptions from many existing sources.
Turn each query, agent, and observed success signal into a unified positive interaction record.
Represent each agent by the tasks, tools, and behaviors it supports.
Evaluate whether a method can map a narrative query to the right deployable agent.
Check how performance changes when many agents appear rarely instead of being chosen many times.

paras: The paper changes the unit of evaluation. Instead of asking whether one component scores well in isolation, it asks whether a system can recommend the right end-to-end agent configuration for a narrative user request.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: how much request meaning overlaps with agent capability
hidden.name: Intent-capability match
paras: Intent-capability match is the amount of overlap between what the user is asking for and what a candidate agent can actually do. This overlap matters more than raw popularity when supervision is long-tail, because the correct agent may appear only a few times in the data.

The benchmark reveals this hidden quantity by aligning narrative queries with capability profiles. If the query needs browsing plus code editing plus structured output, the right agent is the one whose profile contains that combination. Recommendation improves when methods read both sides in content form, because matching meaning is more reliable than memorizing frequently reused identifiers.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the content signals that matter when the right agent is not a frequently repeated favorite.

reads.html: The recommender should succeed because it understands what the request asks for and what each agent can do, not because one agent happens to be famous.
The benchmark shows that long-tail supervision weakens identifier-based recommendation and favors content-aware matching between narrative intent and capability profiles.

mechanism.h2: Why a unified recommendation benchmark matters
paras: The benchmark matters because agent selection happens at the system level. A user does not care whether one language model or one tool router scores well in isolation; the user cares whether the full deployed agent can do the requested job. Evaluating recommendation directly makes the research target match that practical decision.

The data construction is important because no single existing source contains enough query-conditioned agent choices. AgentSelect unifies many fragmented artifacts into one interaction table, which creates training and evaluation data for recommendation methods. That matters because it lets researchers compare approaches on the same task definition instead of on incompatible leaderboards.

The long-tail finding explains why content-aware methods help because many agents appear only rarely, so memorizing identifiers is weak supervision. Reading the request and the capability profile is stronger because the meaning of the job changes smoothly across queries even when the exact agent names do not repeat often.

stages.s: Narrative user request plus candidate agent profiles
Unify many source artifacts into query-agent interactions
Represent each agent by capabilities and tools
Score how well each profile matches the request

math.words: A recommendation method assigns a score to each query-agent pair, and good performance means positive interactions receive higher scores than other candidates for the same query.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Query asks for reading documents, using a spreadsheet tool, and drafting a report.
Agent A can write well but has no spreadsheet tool, so its match score is limited.
Agent B has spreadsheet support but weak document handling, so its score is also limited.
Agent C supports document reading, spreadsheet use, and structured reporting, so it receives the highest score.
The recommender succeeds because it matches the request content to the capability profile.

math.note: The benchmark stresses ranking quality under long-tail data, so a method must score rare but suitable agents above popular but incomplete ones.

charts.title: Identifier-heavy recommendation
charts.note: Methods that rely on repeated identifiers work on popular agents but weaken when recommendation must cover rare configurations.

charts.title: Content-aware recommendation
charts.note: Reading query meaning and capability profiles helps on rare agents because the system can infer suitability from content rather than repetition.

items.html: If the agent profile says little about tools or limits, the recommender cannot match requests to actual abilities.

If the benchmark records only successful pairings, some methods may struggle to learn what makes one capable agent better than another closely related one because the data gives little evidence about which near-miss profile should rank lower.
If one source uses formal task descriptions and another uses casual language, methods may overfit to surface style instead of matching the underlying need.

The benchmark is most useful when capability profiles are detailed and source normalization is careful, because then the recommendation task reflects actual deployable agent choice rather than metadata quirks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small marketplace with ten agent profiles and twenty narrative user requests. Give each profile a list of supported actions, tools, and output styles. Train one baseline that uses only agent identifiers and one baseline that reads both the request and the profile text. The demo should show that content-aware ranking does better on rarely selected agents because it can recover the fit between intent and capability even when a profile has almost no interaction history.
demo.closing: The main lesson should be that agent recommendation is a matching problem, because the right choice depends on the request's capability needs rather than on general popularity alone.
